children.text: A small coral island about

across, floating in the sea southwest of Panglao Island, where the sheer coral wall around the island has been managed as a marine protected area since the mid-1980s. Guided snorkeling with sea turtles up close and wall diving are the heart of Bohol hopping tours.
Balicasag Island is a small, round coral island floating in the sea southwest of Panglao Island. It is about
across and roughly 30 hectares in area, so a walk around the shore takes only
30 minutes
, and a white lighthouse rises in the middle of the island. It lies about
6.5km
from the nearest shore of Panglao and about
10km
in a straight line from Alona Beach, where most travelers depart, so the bangka ride takes
30–45 minutes
. The island has a fishing village, a small chapel, and a government-owned dive resort, and its population is said to be around 800.
The real appeal of this island is underwater. A shallow coral shelf stretching
out from the shore sits at a depth of about
before dropping suddenly into a sheer wall, and the north and northwest walls in particular descend to more than
. Fan corals, soft corals, and black corals cover the wall thickly, and the water stays warm year-round at
Around

, a marine conservation program at Silliman University stopped illegal and destructive fishing around the island, turning the waters into a protected area. The Philippine marine protected area database lists the official registration year as

, so the year differs depending on the source. Either way, thanks to more than 40 years of restricted fishing, green sea turtles and hawksbills are not very afraid of people and come into the seagrass beds close to shore, while big schools of jackfish (trevally) circle along the wall.

Most travelers visit the island on a hopping tour that leaves Alona Beach at dawn. The most common route is a half-day trip combining dolphin-watching, snorkeling at Balicasag, and the Virgin Island (Pontod) sandbar, and divers generally do two dives a day at Balicasag. Even weak swimmers can see turtles thanks to life jackets and guides, but the island sits in open water and is strongly affected by waves and swell, so leave some slack in your schedule for the weather.

You meet sea turtles grazing on the seagrass beds off the island's shore in shallow water just a few meters from the beach. Reviews vary on how many turtles you see at a time, from 4–7 to around 15 on a good day. A guide is required, and your time in the water is limited to about
30–45 minutes
Apart from the turtle zone, there is a separate coral zone. You float over a shelf at
depth and look down at the wall that drops sharply to
below the edge. The west coast is off-limits when the waves are high, and the water near the crowded landing beach tends to get cloudy.
This wall starts
off the shore in front of the resort, in shallows only
deep, which makes it a good introduction for beginner divers. There are many caves and crevices, so a flashlight is useful, and you can see big jackfish hanging in the current.
A slope at the northern tip of the island, notable for black coral, which normally lives below
, growing in shallows of around
. The current is strong, so dives go in at slack water with a pickup boat waiting on the surface, and it is most comfortable for Advanced divers and above.
A slope on the south side of the island, where a hard-coral and soft-coral-covered incline runs from
down to around
. You can drift slowly with the current and finish in the shallows, which makes it a popular spot for a second dive, and you often meet turtles and nudibranchs.

Hundreds of jackfish swirling along the wall are Balicasag's signature sight. Your odds are high on a dive, and barracuda, schools of mackerel, clownfish, lionfish, and frogfish are also commonly reported around the island.
Hopping tours leaving Alona Beach at

look for spinner and bottlenose dolphins in the sea between Panglao and Balicasag. They are most active at dawn, but there is no guarantee, and reviews range from more than 30 dolphins on some days to only 4–5 on others. Occasionally a pod of melon-headed whales passes by.
If you land on the island between snorkeling stops, you can look around the white coral-sand beach, the fishing village, the small chapel, and the lighthouse. A walk around the island takes about
30 minutes
, which makes it a good short break, and walking along the shoreline is easier than taking the inland paths.

There is no scheduled passenger ferry to Balicasag, so you go by bangka from Panglao beaches such as Alona Beach. It takes about
30–45 minutes
from Alona, and boats usually leave around
and return around 11 AM. A joiner tour shared with other travelers costs about
per person, and chartering the whole boat costs about

Book through a tour booth, your accommodation, a dive shop, or an online booking site. Beach touts quote high prices at first, so check what is included (environmental fee, snorkel gear, lunch, Virgin Island entry) before agreeing.

Dive trips go by the boat of a licensed dive shop on Alona Beach, and the boat transfer is included in the diving fee. The Panglao municipality caps daily visitor numbers and licensed shops register in advance, so you cannot just walk up and board. The shop usually collects the environmental fee on your behalf.
If you stay at the Balicasag Island Dive Resort on the island, the resort arranges the boat transfer. Contact the resort directly about booking and whether boats are running.
Bohol has no sharply defined dry and wet seasons and rain falls fairly evenly through the year, so conditions at Balicasag depend less on rain than on which monsoon is blowing.
March–May
is the calmest, with hopping tours going out almost every morning, and diving visibility is best from
December–April
, reaching
. Water temperature is
year-round, so a thin suit is enough, though a 3mm suit is more comfortable if you stay in the water long.
From
June–September
the southwest monsoon (Habagat) pushes swell onto Panglao's south coast, making the afternoon sea rough and tour cancellations more frequent. From
December–February
the northeast monsoon (Amihan) stirs up wind, and bangkas to Balicasag are cancelled more often than you might expect. The flattest seas come in the transition periods of
late February–May
and
October
Bohol lies south of the typhoon track, but in
December 2021
Super Typhoon Odette passed directly over it. When a typhoon or tropical depression approaches, the coast guard bars small boats from leaving and tours are cancelled, so if you go in
November–January
, arrange travel insurance and check the refund policy. Early morning is best in the day, and the Bohol tourism office also advises leaving before
and returning before
. In the afternoon the wind picks up and the tide rises, making the sea rough.

On the island there is the Balicasag Island Dive Resort, owned by the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA), so you can spend a night on the island. It is a small resort with cottage-style rooms on about 1.5 hectares; the location is the best, but some reviews mention worn facilities and unreliable water and electricity, so lower your expectations and check its condition before booking. Most people stay at Alona Beach in Panglao and visit for the day, and Alona offers a wide range, from
guesthouses to beach resorts at
and up.

The island has almost no proper restaurants, only beach stalls selling coconut juice and simple snacks. If lunch is not included on your tour boat, bring water and snacks. Since Virgin Island reopened, the vendor stalls there are gone, so you can no longer expect to buy sea urchin or fruit as before. For a proper meal, head back to Alona Beach for a seafood barbecue and Filipino home cooking.
Pay the environmental fee and snorkeling fee in cash. Be sure to check when booking whether the tour price includes the environmental fee, gear, lunch, and Virgin Island entry.
Sea turtles are best seen in the early morning, before group boats crowd in, so the wait is shorter too. Set your departure time so you reach the island around
7 AM
A guide is mandatory for snorkeling, and time in the water is limited. If you are not confident swimming, wear a life jacket and move along holding on to the guide's canoe.
The quality of rental masks is inconsistent, so if possible bring your own mask and snorkel. The engine is loud, so earplugs can help too.
The area in front of the landing beach is crowded with boats, so see the coral zone on the opposite side, as your guide directs, first. The west coast is off-limits on days when the waves are high.
Some days the turtle zone has many jellyfish. A long-sleeved rash guard protects against both stings and sun, and wrap your waterproof camera strap around your wrist.
If you are prone to seasickness, take your medication
30 minutes
before departure. The sea has more swell than it looks, and the signal can be weak, so agree on a meeting time and place with your group in advance.

Even with an Open Water certification, divers need to be careful about depth management on the wall, so use a dive computer, and Advanced level or above is recommended for Black Forest, where the current is strong.
Diving at Balicasag has a daily visitor cap (about 150 people, two dives, according to the notice), and a separate environmental fee of about
applies. In peak season, book with a licensed dive shop a few days ahead.
The sea depends on the weather, so scheduling this on a day with slack rather than the first day of your trip helps you cope with cancellations.
Touching, chasing, or feeding sea turtles, and stepping on or touching coral, are prohibited by marine protected area rules. Keep at least
away from turtles and stay within the zones and time set by your guide.
Control your buoyancy so you don't kick or stand on the coral with your fins, and kick slowly at the surface.
Some sunscreen ingredients harm coral. Use a reef-safe product or wear a rash guard.
Currents at wall diving sites can suddenly strengthen. Stay close to your guide and keep to the planned depth.
In bad weather the coast guard may bar departures and tours can be cancelled. Check the refund policy before you pay.
Hopping boats accelerating to chase dolphins, or several boats surrounding them, cause the animals great stress. Ask your boat driver to keep a distance.
At Virgin Island you must carry your trash back, and there are limits on length of stay and visitor numbers. The rules change often, so check the latest notice.
